summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. The department of Puno stands under all of these measures: they are national in scope, and the sources record no Puno-specific application, exemption or enforcement practice. A trans visitor to Puno should expect the national position to apply, with the practical outcome often decided by front-line staff rather than by any published procedure.

The operative restriction is the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote; its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow exceptions for medical attention, custody, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The same package bans inclusive or 'ambiguous' restroom signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The bill reached the Plenary from the congressional Women and Family Commission, which on 20 February 2025 unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport in Lima.

In practice the restriction is applied by security and facility staff. LGTBIQ activist and journalist Gianna Camacho warns that bathroom access can come to depend on a guard's personal judgement, including demands for identity documents, and notes that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. Reaching a restroom in Puno may therefore involve an identity check with no published standard to appeal to.

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private commercial life as well. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Hate-crime law offers no cover. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded: a 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and between 2020 and 2023 some 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

On 3 December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Speech and association are constrained by the same 2025 package. Vague child-protection articles, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The 2025 restroom provision was drafted and passed in open tension with that standard.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in a legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte dated 15 April 2025, argues that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors state that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. IDEHPUCP separately recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Comparatively, the 2017 repeal left Peru one of only three countries in South America, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law. Cross-border legal protection therefore offers a visitor little practical cushion.

Undercounting shapes the violence picture: Gianna Camacho, co-author of the 2024 report and a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry, so the 54 killings recorded between 2020 and 2023 should be read as a floor rather than a total.
localsOnly:
Residents' daily exposure to the restroom rule is set nationally; the sources describe no Puno-specific enforcement practice, complaint outcome or local authority guidance, so what happens in Puno workplaces, schools, malls and government buildings mirrors whatever discretion front-line staff exercise elsewhere in Peru.

Two protective developments are on record for residents. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Residents who are children face the sharpest application of the April 2025 law: the exceptions to article 5 cover accompanying a child under 12, not the child's own access, and the same package's vague child-protection articles expose residents to censorship of identity-related media, advertising and educational material, alongside a raised obscenity minimum of four years.

Recourse for residents runs through the courts and the Inter-American system rather than the Penal Code, which no longer carries LGBT hate-crime coverage. The Azul Rojas Marín litigation shows that route is possible but slow: nearly 20 years from attack to a 17-year sentence.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records a Puno-specific enforcement action, complaint, arrest, court ruling or act of violence against a trans person. The absence of such a record is unresolved rather than evidence that none occurred.

The inventory does not state how article 5 interacts with identity documents in Puno, whether a visitor's gender marker on a passport or Peruvian entry record affects restroom or facility access, or which authority receives complaints about staff demands for ID. Those points are not sourced here.

Whether the merged bills 6506 and 8457 were enacted as the April 2025 law described by IDEHPUCP, or proceeded through a further legislative step, is not set out in the sources beyond the committee approval of 20 February 2025 and the Plenary approval of 2 April 2025.

Violence figures for 2020 to 2023 and the 2024 hate-crime report are national; no departmental breakdown for Puno is available, so any local rate of violence remains not sourced.
